newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: BASS CZECH UNIT STAYS IN RED DESPITE EXPORT SURGE.
newsitem.headline: BASS CZECH UNIT STAYS IN RED DESPITE EXPORT SURGE.

text.p: Czech brewer Prazske Pivovary (PP) a.s. , majority-owned by Britain's Bass plc , said on Monday that 1996 had been a good year for exports but that heavy investments kept it in the red.
The Prague-based brewer said it posted a 1996 net loss, according to Czech accounting standards of 100 million crowns compared with a 24 million crown loss the previous year.
Despite the losses, the PP said 1996 had been an excellent year for exports, which rose by 60 percent, year-on-year, and that its losses were mainly caused by heavy investments.

"It is all the same very important to build on the results for 1996 when we showed a 60 rise (in exports)," Bass country manager Graham Stealy told journalists adding thatincreasing market share is still the company's the main aim.

"The main strategic goal of the company still remains the strengthening of its position on the Czech beer market," he said. "That means increasing the current 14 percent market share in the next few years to 25 percent, by organic growth and further possible mergers," he added.

Bass took a 33 percent stake in Prazske Pivovary in 1994 and gradually increased its holdings to the current 55 percent. Along the way, Bass bought up two small regional breweries merging them into Prazske Pivovary earlier this year.
The British Brewer also has a 33 percent stake in the Czech Republic's second largest brewery, Radegast where it would also like to increase its holdings.

"The achievement of our aim, for a 25 percent market share, will probably be effected by further acquisitions. Our talks with other Radegast shareholders are continuing and we would like to get more shares," Stealy said.
According to Prazske Pivovary's Financial Director Miroslav Jirsak, the company does not plan to pay a dividend on 1996 results after paying a gross dividend of 14 crowns per share in 1995.
Prazske Pivovary produces some of the Czech Republic's most popular brands, including Staropramen, which is its most heavily-exported beer.
